title: Why culture matters in organizational change
blurb: Explain what culture is, why it can block or enable change, and why a change only sticks when the culture shifts.
question: An insurer's teams adopted stand-ups and iterations, but six months after the project closed they had quietly gone back to the old ways. What was missed, and why does culture matter in OCM?

teach.h: Culture: how things are really done
teach.body: PRINCE2 Project Management describes culture as the set of shared attitudes, values, goals and practices of a group. In plain English, it is 'how things are really done round here', whatever the procedures say. PRINCE2 Agile asks that culture is considered explicitly in organizational change management, because the same new process can thrive in one culture and be quietly ignored in another.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 7 manual 3.2.3; PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.3

teach.h: Culture can block or enable a change
teach.caption: Illustrative contrasts for teaching; the point is that culture decides adoption.

teach.h: Change only sticks when culture shifts
teach.body: When deciding the detail of the change management approach, the book asks you to consider the evolving culture and ways to ensure changes are not rolled back after the transformation. New tools, rules or rewards can start a change, but if the shared values and habits stay the same, people drift back once the project team leaves. Evolving the culture is what makes the target state last.

teach.h: Keeping ways of working aligned with culture
teach.caption: PRINCE2 7 manual 3.2.3: gather and act on feedback so defined ways of working stay aligned with how people actually work.

root.label: Teams keep working around the agreed process

children.label: Ways of working no longer fit the culture: gather feedback, adapt
More audits and rules: compliance while watched

teach.caption: PRINCE2 7 treats persistent non-compliance as a leading indicator of a culture mismatch.

teach.body: Kestrel Mutual, an insurer, is introducing agile in its claims teams. Agile coach Tomasz Wilk notices that claims handlers keep skipping the new triage board. Rather than ordering audits, he holds conversations with the handlers and learns that managers still reward individual case counts, not team flow. The change management approach is updated: team goals replace individual targets, and team values and norms are agreed in the kickoff workshop so the new habits survive after the project closes.

teach.text: Compliance is not culture change. Bonuses, mandates or a single launch message may get people to follow a process while someone is watching, but the book's answer to 'how do we stop it rolling back?' is to evolve the culture. And persistent non-compliance is a signal to listen and adapt, not just to enforce harder.

items: Culture: the shared attitudes, values, goals and practices of a group.
Culture must be considered explicitly in OCM; it can block or enable change.
Change sticks when culture evolves; plan to stop changes rolling back (4.2.1).
Incentives alone cannot guarantee change lasts; balance with purpose and recognition.
Persistent non-compliance is a leading indicator that ways of working do not fit.
Doing agile alone gives short-term efficiency; being agile brings cultural shift.

summary: You can now explain culture as shared attitudes, values, goals and practices, and why it decides whether a change is adopted. You can also say why change sticks only when culture evolves, and how to read non-compliance as a warning sign.

A.q: Which BEST describes culture as PRINCE2 Project Management uses the term?
options: The formal structure chart of the project management team
Shared attitudes, values, goals and practices
The documented procedures in the management approaches
The tolerances delegated by the project board
A.why: Culture is the set of shared attitudes, values, goals and practices (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.2.3).

whyNot.0: A structure chart shows roles and reporting lines, not shared values and habits.
whyNot.2: Documented procedures describe intended ways of working; culture is how people actually behave.
whyNot.3: Tolerances are delegated limits for management by exception.

A.q: After an agile transformation, which is MOST likely to stop the new ways of working being rolled back?
options: A bonus for staff who follow the new process
A policy instructing everyone to use the process
Evolving the culture to support the new ways
A detailed end project report for the board
A.why: Book 4.2.1 links the evolving culture with ensuring changes are not rolled back after the transformation.

whyNot.0: Financial incentives on their own cannot guarantee that changes stay in place.
whyNot.1: An instruction may produce compliance while watched, but not lasting change.
whyNot.3: The end project report reviews the project; it does not embed new behaviour.

A.q: Persistent non-compliance with agreed project processes is a leading indicator that:
options: the ways of working no longer fit the emerging culture
the project has exceeded its agreed time tolerance
the team needs more detailed work package descriptions
the project board should prepare to close the project
A.why: PRINCE2 7 (3.2.3) treats persistent non-compliance as a leading indicator that the agreed ways of working no longer fit the emerging culture.

whyNot.1: Time tolerance is about forecast schedule, not whether people follow processes.
whyNot.2: More detailed work packages tighten control but do not address the culture mismatch.
whyNot.3: Closure is decided on business grounds, not because people bypass a process.

B.q:
Which two statements about culture in organizational change are correct?
1. Culture is the set of shared attitudes, values, goals and practices.
2. Financial incentives by themselves can guarantee that new behaviours stay in place.
3. The change management approach should consider the evolving culture.
4. Culture is outside a project's influence, so OCM ignores it.
options: 1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
1 and 3
B.why: Culture is shared attitudes, values, goals and practices (PRINCE2 7 3.2.3), and the change management approach should consider the evolving culture (book 4.2.1).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: incentives alone cannot guarantee that changes stay in place.
whyNot.1: Both are wrong: incentives alone do not guarantee change, and the change management approach considers the evolving culture (4.2.1).
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is wrong: the change management approach considers the evolving culture and how to stop changes rolling back (4.2.1).

B.q: A team follows the new agile process when the auditor visits, but nobody understands why the steps exist. This is MOST like:
options: doing agile without being agile
being agile without doing agile
trading and swapping backlog items
applying the manage by exception principle
B.why: Doing agile is applying frameworks, techniques and terms; doing it alone can mean following a framework rigidly without knowing the why, with no lasting impact (2.3.1).

whyNot.1: Being agile is the mindset; here the mindset is exactly what is missing.
whyNot.2: Trading and swapping exchanges backlog items of similar effort; it is unrelated.
whyNot.3: Manage by exception is about delegated tolerances, not process compliance.

B.q: Teams keep working around the agreed process for approving designs. What is the BEST first response?
options: Raise an exception report to the project board
Add audits so that the process is enforced
Gather feedback and adapt the ways of working
Record each case in the risk register and continue
B.why: PRINCE2 7 (3.2.3) says to gather and act on feedback so defined ways of working stay aligned with how people actually work; persistent non-compliance signals a mismatch.

whyNot.0: An exception report is for forecasts beyond tolerance, not for a ways-of-working mismatch.
whyNot.1: Audits may force compliance while watched, but do not fix the mismatch with culture.
whyNot.3: Logging and carrying on ignores the signal that the process does not fit.

C.q: Which project kickoff workshop topic is aimed MOST directly at building an agile culture?
options: Team skill matrix
Project dashboard
Team values and norms
Icebreaker and introductions
C.why: In the project kickoff workshop (Table 13.8), the team values and norms topic sets agile culture and expectations.

whyNot.0: The team skill matrix maps skills, gaps and overlaps.
whyNot.1: The project dashboard is created for transparency of project progress.
whyNot.3: The icebreaker builds familiarity and connections, not the team's values.

C.q: A sponsor proposes a points-based reward scheme as the main way to make agile working last. Why is this weak?
options: Rewards need a formal change request through the issues practice
Peer-assessed rewards conflict with project assurance duties
Rewards belong in the benefits management approach instead
Incentives on their own cannot guarantee that behaviours last
C.why: Financial incentives alone cannot guarantee that changes stay in place (book 4.5); the change must be embedded by evolving the culture (4.2.1).

whyNot.0: Reward schemes are not baseline changes handled through the issues practice.
whyNot.1: Project assurance monitors governance; it has no conflict with peer rewards.
whyNot.2: The benefits management approach covers benefits actions and reviews, not staff rewards.

C.q: How does being agile differ from doing agile in its effect on an organization?
options: Being agile brings cultural shift; doing agile alone gives short-term gains
Being agile is the framework; doing agile is the underlying mindset
Being agile applies to delivery teams; doing agile applies to the project board
Being agile removes the need for any processes or practices
C.why: Book 2.3.1: being agile creates cultural shift and long-term resilience; doing agile alone gives short-term efficiency without lasting impact.

whyNot.1: This reverses them: doing agile is frameworks and terms; being agile is the mindset.
whyNot.2: Both apply at every level; they are not split by role.
whyNot.3: Being agile still uses structure; being without any doing lacks structure.

reteach.title: The office recycling bins
reteach.question: Why do new recycling bins sometimes fill with general rubbish a month after the launch email?

blocks.body: A facilities team installs new bins and sends a launch email. For a week, people sort carefully. Then old habits return, because nothing about what people value or expect of each other has changed. If team leads model it, colleagues remind each other, and the reasons are understood, the habit holds. That shift in shared values and practice is culture, and it is what makes any change stick.

blocks.text: A reward or an instruction can start a change, but it is the evolving culture that stops it rolling back.

explain.body: Culture is the set of shared attitudes, values, goals and practices of a group: how things are really done, not what the procedure says.

test.q: In PRINCE2 Project Management, culture is the set of shared:
options: tolerances, plans, reports and registers
attitudes, values, goals and practices
roles, responsibilities and reporting lines
products, quality criteria and acceptors
test.why: Culture is the set of shared attitudes, values, goals and practices (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.2.3).

whyNot.0: These are management products and controls, not culture.
whyNot.2: Roles and reporting lines are defined in the organization practice.
whyNot.3: Products and quality criteria belong to the quality practice.

explain.body: Gather and act on feedback so the defined ways of working stay aligned with how people actually work. If they drift apart, people quietly work around the process.

test.q: Why should a project gather feedback on how people actually work?
options: To decide which team members to replace or retrain
To keep defined ways of working aligned with real practice
To fill in the quality register entry for each product
To set the project's time and cost tolerances for each stage
test.why: Feedback keeps the defined ways of working aligned with how people actually work (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.2.3).

whyNot.0: The aim is to adapt ways of working, not to replace people.
whyNot.2: The quality register records quality activities and results.
whyNot.3: Stage tolerances are set by the project board; feedback on ways of working does not set them.

explain.body: The change management approach should consider the evolving culture and ways to ensure changes are not rolled back after the transformation (book 4.2.1).

test.q: When deciding the detail of the change management approach, book 4.2.1 suggests considering:
options: the order of the stage boundaries
the tolerance for extra cost per stage
ways to ensure changes are not rolled back
the format of the project product description
test.why: Book 4.2.1 lists the evolving culture and ways to ensure changes are not rolled back after the transformation.

whyNot.0: Stage boundaries are set in the plans and progress practices.
whyNot.1: PRINCE2 Agile sets zero tolerance for extra cost; it is not a change management consideration.
whyNot.3: The project product description is tailored into the project backlog; it is not an OCM consideration.

explain.body: Doing agile is applying frameworks, techniques and terminology. Being agile is thinking in an agile way and being allowed to apply it. Doing alone gives short-term efficiency; being creates cultural shift.

test.q: Which brings cultural shift and long-term resilience?
options: Adding more stand-ups
Doing agile
Renaming the roles
Being agile
test.why: Book 2.3.1: being agile creates cultural shift and long-term resilience.

whyNot.0: More meetings are a practice change, not a change in mindset.
whyNot.1: Doing agile alone gives short-term efficiency without lasting impact.
whyNot.2: New role names change terminology, not culture.
